commons:144186874.summary: The jewelled cover of Emperor Henry II's book of Gospel readings frames an older ivory of the Crucifixion within gold, gems, pearls and enamel roundels of the evangelists' symbols. In the ivory, angels hover above the cross between the sun and moon, mourners and soldiers stand below, the holy women come to the tomb, and the dead rise from their graves, with Ocean and Earth at the bottom. The Ottonian goldsmiths thus enshrined a Carolingian masterpiece, honouring the crucified Christ with the most precious materials of the age.
facts: Wikipedia notes that the ivory plaque was carved around 870, probably in the circle of the Carolingian court school associated with Metz, and was reused in the 11th-century cover.
The manuscript, made for Henry II, the last Ottonian emperor, is a masterpiece of the Reichenau 'Liuthar group' of illuminators; it is now Clm 4452 in the Bavarian State Library.
The cover's inscription names Henry II; the Commons description links its making to the founding of the diocese of Bamberg in 1007.
commons:144186874.notes: Dating of the frame varies: Wikipedia gives c. 1014, the Commons description c. 1007 (foundation of Bamberg). Wikipedia also says Christ and the twelve apostles appear along the frame; this could not be confirmed at thumbnail size.

cur:catacombs-bargello-peter-paul-crowne.summary: The bearded busts of Peter and Paul, named in gold letters, face each other while a small standing Christ between them holds wreaths over their heads. A Latin toast runs around the rim, recalling that these were once the bottoms of drinking bowls.
facts: The image of Christ crowning Peter and Paul is common on Roman gold glass, reflecting the cult of the two apostles in Rome.
It was exhibited at 'Pretiosa vitrea', Florence, 2017–2018.

cur:catacombs-parma-christ-twelve-apostl.summary: In the central roundel is a bust of Christ, and around it, like rays, stand the twelve apostles, some named in gold letters such as PETRUS. The radiating composition places Christ at the centre of the apostolic college, as the sun among its rays.
facts: Commons places it in the collections of the National Archaeological Museum of Parma and dates it to the 4th–5th century.
cur:catacombs-parma-christ-twelve-apostl.notes: The identification of the central bust as Christ follows the museum's title; the glass is cracked.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-128-chris.summary: On a hillock at the right, a personification of Israel or Sion with three of the faithful appeals to the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, who appears in a mandorla with angels and hands a sword to an angel leading an attack on her oppressors: 'many a time have they afflicted me from my youth'. Men with mattocks threaten to plough furrows on her back, and at the left grass is cut and burned, 'as the grass upon the housetops'. The drawing illustrates a psalm of endurance.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
It reached Canterbury by about 1000, where it was copied three times in the Middle Ages: the Harley Psalter, the Eadwine Psalter and the Anglo-Catalan Psalter.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-128-chris.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-jairus-woman-i.summary: Beneath a great ornamental arch Christ, followed by two apostles, stretches out his hand toward the bed on which the girl lies, watched by her father and the women of the house; at his feet a small kneeling woman touches the hem of his robe. The painter combines the two interwoven miracles of Matthew's Gospel in a single scene.
facts: The Gospels of Otto III has 276 leaves, twelve canon tables, a double-page portrait of the emperor, four evangelist portraits and 29 full-page miniatures of New Testament scenes; it was produced at Reichenau around 1000.
Its original cover still holds a 10th-century Byzantine ivory of the Dormition of the Virgin.
cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-jairus-woman-i.notes: Identification inferred from the composition and from the place of the page in Matthew's Gospel (fol. 44r). Folio derived from the BSB image sequence (image 91); verify against the foliation on the page.

cur:manuscripts2-valcavado-lord-worshipp.summary: In a large circle at the upper left sits the Lord enthroned, holding a book, while the elders bow before him and an angel sounds the seventh trumpet; below, the story of the two witnesses unfolds — their bodies lying in the street, and their ascent to heaven. The elders' hymn, 'We give thee thanks, O Lord God Almighty', is the climax of the page.
facts: The Valcavado Beatus was written and illuminated in 970 by the monk Oveco for Abbot Sempronius of Valcavado, in the reign of Ramiro III of León; it has 230 surviving leaves and 87 miniatures.
Beatus of Liébana compiled his Commentary on the Apocalypse in the late 8th century; its illustrated copies form one of the great cycles of early Spanish painting.
cur:manuscripts2-valcavado-lord-worshipp.notes: The enthroned figure is identified with Christ following the Beatus tradition; Revelation 11:17 addresses 'the Lord God Almighty'.

cur:monumental-oberzell-gerasene.summary: At the left, Christ, haloed and followed by apostles, raises his hand towards the possessed man, while to the right the demons enter the herd of swine, which rushes headlong down into the blue water beneath a walled town. As the first scene of the cycle, by the entrance, it opens the story of Christ's power over evil.
facts: The eight miracle scenes on the nave walls of St George, Oberzell, were rediscovered under later plaster in 1880; they are dated either to about 900 (late Carolingian) or, in the prevailing view, to the late 10th century (Ottonian).

Apart from Müstair, St George is the only church north of the Alps in the former Empire to preserve so complete a cycle of early medieval wall painting; the sequence runs from the entrance along the north wall to the altar and back along the south wall, culminating in the Raising of Lazarus.
The German Wikipedia notes a possible parallel with the founding legend of Reichenau, in which Bishop Pirmin arrived by boat and drove serpents and demons from the island.

vam:O96313.summary: Carved in high relief from a slab of green, red-flecked jasper, Christ hangs on the cross in a long loincloth, his feet nailed separately to a footrest, with the Sun and Moon above the arms of the cross. The Virgin stands at his right, raising her mantle-covered hand towards him, and St John stands at his left holding a scroll. Worn at the breast, this luxurious little image would have been the focus of its owner's prayers.
facts: The inscription IC XC (Jesus Christ) is carved on the plaque above Christ's head, and a further inscription is translated by the V&A as 'is crucified'.
The suspension loop is not original, but the V&A believes it reflects the pendant's original use as an enkolpion, a sacred image worn on the breast.
It was bought from the Venetian dealer Adolph Loewi, who had acquired it from a private family in Rome; it may be one of many portable Byzantine objects that reached Italy before the 15th century.
vam:O96313.notes: Byzantine (Constantinople), ca. 900 (V&A). Purchased under the Bequest of Francis Reubell Bryan (A.77-1937).

Q568847.summary: Ten nearly life-size figures crowd a shallow gilded niche like painted sculpture as Christ's body is lowered from the cross. The Virgin, swooning, falls in a curve that mirrors the pose of her dead Son — a visual expression of her 'co-suffering' with him. Every tear, fabric and gesture is rendered with piercing realism, making this one of the most emotionally powerful paintings of the 15th century.
facts: Tiny crossbows painted in the corner tracery honor the Greater Guild of Crossbowmen of Leuven, who commissioned the work for their chapel of Our Lady Without the Walls.
Around 1548 Mary of Hungary acquired it in exchange for a copy and an organ; her nephew Philip II took it to Spain, where it hung at the Escorial until entering the Prado in 1939.
It was copied repeatedly — the copy given to Leuven was by Michiel Coxcie — and Otto von Simson claimed no other painting of its school was copied or adapted so often.
The shape of the panel, with its raised central section and gilded tracery, evokes a carved and painted altarpiece shrine.

Q235242.summary: The Virgin Mary holds the dead Christ across her lap, her face serene and youthful, her left hand opened in a gesture of offering and acceptance. Michelangelo, then in his early twenties, carved the group from a single block, balancing tenderness and idealised beauty with profound grief.
facts: It was commissioned by the French cardinal Jean de Bilhères for his funerary chapel.
It is the only work Michelangelo ever signed; his name is carved across the sash on Mary's chest.
Mary's youthfulness, criticised by some, was explained by Michelangelo as a sign of her purity.
The statue was damaged by a hammer-wielding attacker in 1972 and has since been displayed behind protective glass.
